script.title: Mean vs Median vs Mode explained simply
script.caption_hook: Three averages, one winner each. Which one do you pick?

lines.say: Ma'am, why do we need three averages? One isn't enough?
Each tells a different story. Mean shares equally, median is the middle one, mode is the most popular.
Can you show with an example?
Five employees earn ₹10,000, ₹12,000, ₹12,000, ₹14,000 and ₹52,000 per month.
So mean is just total divided by five?
Yes. Total is ₹1,00,000, divided by five, so the mean is ₹20,000.
But nobody earns ₹20,000 here! That feels wrong.
Exactly. One big salary drags the mean up. Arrange in order, and the median, the middle value, is ₹12,000.
Right. Mode is the most frequent value: ₹12,000, twice. Data can have no mode, or several.
Is there any link between the three?
Yes. Mode equals three times median minus two times mean, for moderately skewed data. If symmetrical, all three are equal.
So when do I pick median over mean?
With outliers or open-ended classes, choose median. For most common or most frequent, choose mode.
Remember: mean meets all, median is middle, mode is most popular.

check_notes: Writer: Example: 10,12,12,14,52 (₹ thousand per month): sum 1,00,000, mean 20,000, median 12,000, mode 12,000. right_on 'median' is a word in line 8. Word count may be near the upper limit.
Checker: Line 15 voice and board (mnemonic 'mean meets all'): the wording is vague and doesn't say what it means. Suggested: 'Mean uses all values, median is the middle, mode is the most frequent.'
Checker: Line 2 board sub 'three averages, one winner each': the wording is unclear and suggests competition rather than suitability. Suggested: 'three averages, each suited to different data'.

Checker: Line 12 board sub 'Only for moderately skewed data': 'Only' is too strong, because the relation also holds trivially for symmetrical data. Also, the formula is approximate and doesn't fit this five-salary example (3×12,000 − 2×20,000 = −4,000, not 12,000), and students might try it. Suggested: 'Approximate; holds for moderately skewed distributions (not small raw data sets like this one)'.
